betaSandwich

Ivan Jacob Agaloos Pesigan 2026-11-15

Description

Generates robust confidence intervals for standardized regression coefficients using heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors for models fitted by lm() as described in Dudgeon (2017: http://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-017-9563-z). Sampling covariance matrices can also be obtained under multivariate normal theory and the asymptotically distribution-free approach. The package can also be used to generate confidence intervals for R-squared, adjusted R-squared, differences of standardized regression coefficients, semipartial correlations, squared partial correlations, the improvement in R-squared, and Cohen’s f-squared. A description of the package and code examples are presented in Pesigan, Sun, and Cheung (2023: https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2023.2201277).

Installation

You can install the CRAN release of betaSandwich with:

install.packages("betaSandwich")

You can install the development version of betaSandwich from GitHub with:

if (!require("pak")) install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("jeksterslab/betaSandwich")

Example

In this example, a multiple regression model is fitted using program quality ratings (QUALITY) as the regressand/outcome variable and number of published articles attributed to the program faculty members (NARTIC), percent of faculty members holding research grants (PCTGRT), and percentage of program graduates who received support (PCTSUPP) as regressor/predictor variables using a data set from 1982 ratings of 46 doctoral programs in psychology in the USA (National Research Council, 1982). Robust confidence intervals for the standardized regression coefficients are generated using the BetaHC() function from the betaSandwich package following Dudgeon (2017).

library(betaSandwich)
df <- betaSandwich::nas1982

Fit the regression model using the lm() function. 

object <- lm(QUALITY ~ NARTIC + PCTGRT + PCTSUPP, data = df)

Estimate the standardized regression slopes and the corresponding robust sampling covariance matrix. 

BetaHC(object, type = "hc3", alpha = 0.05)
#> Call:
#> BetaHC(object = object, type = "hc3", alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Standardized regression slopes with HC3 standard errors:
#>            est     se      t df      p   2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.4951 0.0786 6.3025 42 0.0000 0.3366 0.6537
#> PCTGRT  0.3915 0.0818 4.7831 42 0.0000 0.2263 0.5567
#> PCTSUPP 0.2632 0.0855 3.0786 42 0.0037 0.0907 0.4358

Other Features

The package provides the following functions.

Function Purpose
BetaHC() Standardized regression coefficients with a heteroskedasticity-consistent sampling covariance matrix (HC0-HC5)
BetaADF() Standardized regression coefficients with an asymptotically distribution-free sampling covariance matrix
BetaN() Standardized regression coefficients with a multivariate normal-theory sampling covariance matrix
RSqSandwich() R-squared and adjusted R-squared
DiffBetaSandwich() Differences of standardized regression coefficients
SCorSandwich() Semipartial correlations
SCorSqSandwich() Squared semipartial correlations (squared signed interval)
PCorSandwich() Squared partial correlations
DeltaRSqSandwich() Improvement in R-squared
FSqSandwich() Cohen’s f-squared and local f-squared

The coef(), vcov(), confint(), summary(), and print() methods are available for the returned objects. Examples for each function are in the package vignettes.

Effect Sizes

Let \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast} be the vector of standardized slopes, \mathbf{R}_{x} the correlation matrix of the regressors, r^{jj} the jth diagonal element of \mathbf{R}_{x}^{-1}, n the sample size, and k the number of parameters of the regression model, including the intercept. Each effect size below is a function g\left( \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast} \right) of the standardized parameters. Its sampling variance is approximated by the delta method,

\widehat{\mathrm{var}} \left( \hat{g} \right) = \mathbf{J}_{g} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast}} \mathbf{J}_{g}^{\prime},

where \mathbf{J}_{g} is the Jacobian of g and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast}} is the sampling covariance matrix from BetaHC(), BetaADF(), or BetaN() (Yuan & Chan, 2011). The three functions differ in the estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the sample covariances. BetaN() assumes multivariate normality (Browne, 1984). BetaADF() uses sample fourth moments and requires only that they exist, but it is noisy in small samples (Browne, 1984; Jones & Waller, 2015). BetaHC() keeps the normal-theory model for the regressors but replaces the assumption of constant error variance with the squared residuals of the cases (HC0 to HC5) (Cribari-Neto, 2004; Dudgeon, 2017; MacKinnon & White, 1985; White, 1980), and it is recommended in most situations. Confidence intervals are \hat{g} \pm z_{1 - \alpha / 2} \, \widehat{\mathrm{se}} \left( \hat{g} \right).

R-squared and adjusted R-squared (RSqSandwich())

R^{2} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast\prime} \mathbf{R}_{x} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast}, \quad \bar{R}^{2} = 1 - \left( 1 - R^{2} \right) \frac{n - 1}{n - k}.

R^{2} is the proportion of the variance of the outcome explained by the regressors. \bar{R}^{2} corrects R^{2} for the number of regressors.

Semipartial correlation (SCorSandwich())

sr_{j} = \frac{\beta^{\ast}_{j}}{\sqrt{r^{jj}}} = \beta^{\ast}_{j} \sqrt{1 - R^{2}_{j \cdot -j}},

where R^{2}_{j \cdot -j} is the R-squared from regressing regressor j on the other regressors. It is the correlation between the outcome and the part of regressor j that is not explained by the other regressors. Because 1 / r^{jj} = 1 - R^{2}_{j \cdot -j}, sr_{j} shrinks toward zero as regressor j becomes more redundant with the other regressors, even when \beta^{\ast}_{j} does not.

Improvement in R-squared (DeltaRSqSandwich())

\Delta R^{2}_{j} = R^{2} - R^{2}_{-j} = sr^{2}_{j}.

It is the change in R^{2} when regressor j is added last, the proportion of the variance of the outcome that regressor j alone accounts for.

Squared semipartial correlation interval (SCorSqSandwich())

The interval \left[ l, u \right] of the signed sr_{j} is squared as a set. The result is \left[ l^{2}, u^{2} \right] if 0 < l, \left[ u^{2}, l^{2} \right] if u < 0, and \left[ 0, \max \left( l^{2}, u^{2} \right) \right] if the interval contains zero. This is not the delta-method interval of DeltaRSqSandwich().

Squared partial correlation (PCorSandwich())

pr^{2}_{j} = \frac{sr^{2}_{j}}{1 - R^{2} + sr^{2}_{j}}.

It is the proportion of the variance of the outcome not explained by the other regressors that is explained by regressor j.

Cohen’s f-squared and local f-squared (FSqSandwich())

f^{2} = \frac{R^{2}}{1 - R^{2}}, \quad f^{2}_{j} = \frac{sr^{2}_{j}}{1 - R^{2}}.

By convention (Cohen, 1988), values of about 0.02, 0.15, and 0.35 are small, medium, and large effects.

Differences of standardized slopes (DiffBetaSandwich())

\beta^{\ast}_{j} - \beta^{\ast}_{l}.

It compares the standardized effects of regressors j and l on the same scale.

Effect sizes near zero

\beta^{\ast}_{j} and sr_{j} are signed and have no boundary at zero. R^{2}, \Delta R^{2}_{j}, pr^{2}_{j}, and f^{2}_{j} cannot be negative. When the population value is zero, the gradient of the squared effect sizes is zero, the first-order delta-method variance vanishes, and a symmetric Wald interval is not justified. Near zero, the sampling distribution remains skewed and bounded in finite samples, and the interval can extend below zero. An interval for sr_{j} can therefore behave well where the interval for sr^{2}_{j} does not. SCorSqSandwich() respects the bound by squaring the interval of sr_{j} as a set.
